cl_alc_water_dehydration.q: Is a hangover just being thirsty, and does drinking water fix it?
cl_alc_water_dehydration.short: Not just thirst, it seems. Thirst was clearly up only in the morning, but the hangover lasted all day. No experiment had tested water by mid-2024.
cl_alc_water_dehydration.but: It all comes from one review, partly its authors' second look at their own data.
how: Small old studies found mild, brief changes in body fluids after drinking. The review's authors think being dried out and a hangover are separate effects.
Among 176 people with a hangover on a long walk, those who felt worse drank more water. But drinking more didn't go with getting better faster.
In student surveys, water was the most used hangover remedy. Students gave it about 5 to 6 out of 10 for how well it worked.
cl_alc_water_dehydration.rate: It's all from one review: a walk in the heat where people who felt worse drank more water, students' own ratings, and small, old lab studies of men. No experiment tested water itself.

cl_alc_protective_strategies.q: Do habits meant to make drinking less harmful help?
cl_alc_protective_strategies.short: Not clearly. Teaching students bundles of habits, like pacing or eating, barely changed their drinking, by their own account. No trial tested one habit alone.
cl_alc_protective_strategies.but: Nearly all were US college students. And every result is what they said about themselves.
how: In trials, how much students said they drank didn't clearly change. They said they drank very slightly less often, and may have had very slightly fewer problems from drinking.
A 2013 review says students reporting more habits nearly always reported drinking less or fewer problems. But most were asked about both at one sitting.
Day by day, students reported drinking more on days with a designated driver or a friend to go home with. The review's author thinks those are planned for heavy nights.
cl_alc_protective_strategies.rate: The trials agree, but 14 of 15 had weaknesses, every result was self-reported, and nearly all were US students. Habits were taught in bundles, often with other parts, so no single habit was tested.

cl_opi_loperamide_withdrawal.q: Does loperamide help with opioid withdrawal?
cl_opi_loperamide_withdrawal.short: We can't say. The one study we read didn't check if loperamide eased opioid withdrawal.
cl_opi_loperamide_withdrawal.but: It only counted people who saw a poisons doctor. And it had no group to compare them with.
how: A US registry counted 26 people seen by poisons doctors after taking loperamide. Six of them took it to avoid withdrawal.
It recorded the problems that brought people to care, not whether their withdrawal eased.
The authors think a lack of methadone or buprenorphine treatment may be part of why people take it for withdrawal. The study didn't measure that.
cl_opi_loperamide_withdrawal.rate: One small registry of people who needed a poisons doctor. It never measured whether withdrawal eased, and it had no one to compare with.

cl_benzo_own_practices.q: Do people's own habits lower the harms of benzos?
cl_benzo_own_practices.short: Nobody knows yet. A 2025 review of benzo harm reduction found no study that checked whether any habit lowers harm.
cl_benzo_own_practices.but: It's what people said and what researchers suggest, from one review. It didn't check how good its sources were.
how: People on a Swedish forum about flubromazolam, a newer benzo, wrote of staying home. They also wrote of keeping it out of reach while high, and not drinking with it.
In Canada, women and gender-diverse people who use drugs set up friend groups to check on each other. They feared benzos in their drugs, and sexual assault.
People whose test strip found fentanyl reported taking more care, like keeping naloxone nearby. That's a medicine for opioid overdose. The link was strongest when they tested benzos.
cl_benzo_own_practices.rate: It's second-hand, from one review that didn't check how good its sources were: forum posts, people's accounts, a survey and two test-strip studies. None tested whether a habit lowers harm.

cl_xc_coping_during.q: What helps people get through a difficult psychedelic trip?
cl_xc_coping_during.short: Looking back, people most often say letting go or calming the mind helped them through a hard psychedelic trip. None of it was tested.
cl_xc_coping_during.but: These are memories, sometimes years old, from people who chose to answer. Saying something helped may just reflect how the trip ended.
how: In an online survey, 529 people recalled a hard trip on a classic psychedelic, like psilocybin or LSD. 85 in 100 had tried letting go and found it helpful.
Least often tried and found helpful were getting angry at it and trying to sleep. Taking another drug or a drink was near the bottom too.
In a US survey, trying to calm the mind was ticked as helpful most often. Next came changing place and asking a friend for help.
cl_xc_coping_during.rate: Only what people remembered, sometimes years later, in people who chose to answer, with nothing tested. Two separate surveys agree on what's named most, but they asked different questions.

cl_xc_harm_reduction_habits.q: Do harm reduction habits mean fewer difficult psychedelic trips?
cl_xc_harm_reduction_habits.short: Nobody can say yet. In one survey, a higher score for safety habits went with a slightly easier first psychedelic trip. Not clearly the latest, though.
cl_xc_harm_reduction_habits.but: People recalled habits and trips at one sitting, often years later. And people who quit after a hard first trip couldn't take part.
how: 163 experienced people, mostly men, recalled their first and latest trip. They said which safety habits they'd used and how hard each trip was.
A higher habit score also went with more emotional breakthrough on both trips. All these links were weak.
Most were with trusted friends. Few had a sober sitter or tested their drugs, though the group rated testing as important.
In a US survey, 30 in 100 people linked their hardest trip to having had no preparation. They rated that trip slightly harder.
cl_xc_harm_reduction_habits.rate: One survey of memories that even counted habits after a trip, though they can't change how it went, and took nothing else into account. People who quit after a hard first trip couldn't take part; a review found little other research.

cl_pop_eye_stopping.q: If poppers hurt my eyes, does stopping them or lutein help?
cl_pop_eye_stopping.short: Nobody knows yet, for either. Eye scans improved in 46 of 75 people checked again, but no report compared stopping poppers with carrying on.
cl_pop_eye_stopping.but: These are case reports with no comparison group. Whether people really stopped was recorded for only 27 of 113.
how: In a review of case reports, almost everyone whose treatment was recorded was told to stop poppers. Whether stopping helped vision couldn't be analysed.
Of the two followed longest, the one said to have kept using had no change in vision. The other improved, but nobody recorded whether they'd stopped.
Some earlier reports saw no improvement in the first months, even in people who stopped.
Lutein, a supplement, went to only 5 people, with nobody to compare them with.
cl_pop_eye_stopping.rate: Case reports pooled by one review, with no comparison group. Whether people stopped was recorded for 27 of 113, lutein went to 5, and the improvement may have come anyway.

cl_opi_constipation_otc_laxatives.q: Do ordinary laxatives from the shop help constipation caused by opioids?
cl_opi_constipation_otc_laxatives.short: We can't say yet. The one review we read on opioid constipation had no trials of laxatives from the shop.
cl_opi_constipation_otc_laxatives.but: What we read has no data on it, only its authors' remarks. One of them rests on two reviews we haven't read.
how: The review pooled trials of prescription medicines only. Its authors write that people often try shop laxatives first.
But they say the studies so far make the effect of shop laxatives hard to judge.
They also write that prescription laxatives may not work better than shop ones. They didn't test this.
cl_opi_constipation_otc_laxatives.rate: There's no data on this in what we read: the review didn't include shop laxatives, and its authors' remark is second-hand, from two reviews of laxatives in seriously ill people.

cl_mph_insomnia_sleep_hygiene.q: Do bedtime routines help children on ADHD stimulants fall asleep?
cl_mph_insomnia_sleep_hygiene.short: Maybe a little. With a set routine, children on ADHD stimulants fell asleep in 69 minutes on average, down from 92. Most still took at least an hour.
cl_mph_insomnia_sleep_hygiene.but: There was no comparison group, so part of the change may have happened anyway. For example, children were picked when their sleep was at its worst.
how: The children were 6 to 14 and took over an hour to fall asleep. The routine meant regular bed and wake times, no caffeine and no naps.
Wrist monitors showed a similar drop. But only 5 of about 28 children then fell asleep within an hour.
Clinicians rated 21 in 100 children much or very much better and 54 in 100 unchanged. ADHD ratings didn't change.
cl_mph_insomnia_sleep_hygiene.rate: One small study, comparing children only with their own sleep before. Children were picked when sleep was at its worst, and there was no comparison group, so some of the gain may have come anyway.
